title: What Is OS/2? — Definition
body:
Classic software is the programs that defined personal computing before the modern era: VisiCalc and Lotus 1-2-3 (spreadsheets), WordStar and WordPerfect (word processing), dBase (databases), CP/M and MS-DOS (operating systems), early Windows and Mac System, HyperCard, and the games and utilities that taught the world what software could be.

In the context of this database, the OS/2 is presented as one classic software record among the classic software family. 1987's joint OS: the 286's protected mode — the 'better DOS than DOS'.

title: Origins and History of OS/2
body:
The OS/2 belongs to the 1987–2001 era and traces to IBM/Microsoft.

Software was once free with hardware; IBM's 1969 unbundling created the industry. VisiCalc (1979) sold Apple IIs as business machines; Lotus 1-2-3 (1983) sold IBM PCs. WordStar (1978) and WordPerfect (1982) fought the word-processing wars with function-key templates. dBase II (1981) put databases on desks. CP/M (1974) standardized microcomputer OSes until MS-DOS (1981) and the IBM PC swept it away. The Mac (1984) and Windows 3.0 (1990) brought GUIs mainstream; HyperCard (1987) previewed hypermedia. Shareware (Apogee, id) invented try-before-you-buy distribution over BBSes.

Within that longer story, OS/2: The Workplace Shell; the IBM/Microsoft split. The OS/2 is the also-ran's quality.

title: How OS/2 Works
body:
Early PC software ran in 640K of RAM under DOS, talking directly to hardware (video memory at 0xB800, BIOS interrupts) for speed. Spreadsheets recalculated cell dependency graphs; word processors managed text buffers with printer control codes; databases used B-trees and ISAM files. GUIs drew windows, icons, and menus with QuickDraw/GDI, handling mouse events in an event loop. Copy protection used bad sectors, dongles, and manual lookups ('type word 7 on page 12').

Applied to the OS/2 (1987–2001, IBM/Microsoft): The OS/2 is the also-ran's quality.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Anatomy of OS/2 — Components
body:
Every OS/2 is an assembly of the classic software family's standard parts:

• Spreadsheet engine — Cell grid, formula parser, recalc dependency graph.
• Text buffer — Gap buffer or piece table for editing.
• Printer drivers — Escape-code tables per printer model.
• Database engine — ISAM/B-tree storage, query evaluator.
• DOS kernel — File, memory, and interrupt services.
• GUI toolkit — Windows, menus, dialogs, event loop.
• HyperCard stack — Cards, buttons, fields, HyperTalk scripts.
• Installer — Floppy-disk setup programs; serial numbers.
• Manual — The doorstop documentation; copy protection lived here.
• Template / overlay — Keyboard templates and function-key guides.

When examining a surviving OS/2, identify these parts in order: Spreadsheet engine, Text buffer, Printer drivers, Database engine, DOS kernel, GUI toolkit.

title: Classic Software Glossary
body:
The working vocabulary of classic software:

• killer app — The program that sells the hardware (VisiCalc, Lotus).
• shareware — Try-before-you-buy; Apogee's episodic model.
• copy protection — Bad sectors, dongles, manual checks; the arms race.
• TSR — Terminate-and-stay-resident; DOS multitasking hack.
• 640K barrier — DOS conventional memory limit; 'enough for anyone'.
• expanded / extended memory — EMS/XMS tricks to exceed 640K.
• macro — Recorded keystroke automation; Lotus macros ran businesses.
• mail merge — Word processor + database = personalized letters.
• WYSIWYG — What you see is what you get; the GUI promise.
• clipboard — Cut/copy/paste between programs.
• file format wars — .doc vs .wpd vs .txt; converters as diplomacy.
• abandonware — Orphaned software preserved by enthusiasts.

title: OS/2 in Culture
body:
Classic software has a look and feel — the Lotus slash menu, WordPerfect's reveal codes, the DOS prompt's blink — burned into a generation's muscle memory. Shareware taught that software could be a gift economy; BBS file areas were the first app stores. 'Press any key' and 'Abort, Retry, Fail?' are folk sayings. Abandonware archivists keep it all bootable.

The OS/2 carries that cultural charge directly: The OS/2 is the also-ran's quality.

title: Collecting and Preserving OS/2
body:
Boxed software with manuals and disks is the prize; disks need imaging on arrival. Dongles and code wheels complete the story. Keep original media write-protected; run from images. License transfers are murky — collect for preservation and study.

For the OS/2 specifically: 1987's joint OS: the 286's protected mode — the 'better DOS than DOS'.. Prioritize completeness and originality over shine; a working OS/2 with honest wear outranks a polished non-runner.

title: OS/2 Restoration Guide
body:
Image disks with KryoFlux/Greaseweazle before they die. Run in DOSBox/VMs with period-correct settings. Document serial numbers and versions. Scan manuals — the documentation is half the artifact.

Restoration order for a OS/2: 1) document everything photographically before touching it; 2) stabilize (clean, de-corrode, free seized parts); 3) repair before replacing; 4) replace only what is missing or dangerous, marking replacements; 5) test under supervision. Never power an unrestored electrical classic software record without a current-limited bring-up.
